cases.architecture: Socket.IO gateway plus a raw `ws` widget bridge and Express SSE routes for a support desk, over Postgres and Mongo: two sibling deployments (apps/agent-desk and apps/shared-inbox) that share the same module layout.
cases.why: The upgrade is completed for anyone who asks for the right path, and the identity the whole bridge then trusts is read straight off the query string: `agentId` and `orgId` are whatever the connecting client typed. No cookie, token or signature is checked anywhere in this handler, so a stranger can open `/bridge/v1?agent=...&org=<victim org>` and every frame handler downstream - which all scope their reads off `ws.session` - will serve that tenant's data.

cases.architecture: Socket.IO gateway plus a raw `ws` widget bridge and Express SSE routes for a support desk, over Postgres and Mongo: two sibling deployments (apps/agent-desk and apps/shared-inbox) that share the same module layout.
cases.why: The credential also rides on the query string, but it is a ticket the desk API minted: `verifyHandshakeTicket` recomputes the HMAC over the encoded claims with the server-side secret, compares it with `timingSafeEqual`, and rejects anything older than thirty seconds, so the agent and org on the socket are values the server asserted rather than values the client chose. A handshake without a valid ticket is answered with 401 and destroyed.

cases.architecture: Socket.IO gateway plus a raw `ws` widget bridge and Express SSE routes for a support desk, over Postgres and Mongo: two sibling deployments (apps/agent-desk and apps/shared-inbox) that share the same module layout.
cases.why: `frame.term` is client-controlled - the frame arrives as a WebSocket message and is dispatched into this handler by `routeFrame` in bridge/router.js, so the tainted value crosses a module boundary before it gets here - and it is interpolated into a quoted ILIKE literal in the statement text while the org id and limit beside it are properly bound. A quote in the search term closes the literal and the remainder is parsed as SQL, which also defeats the `m.org_id = $1` tenant predicate on the same query.

cases.architecture: Socket.IO gateway plus a raw `ws` widget bridge and Express SSE routes for a support desk, over Postgres and Mongo: two sibling deployments (apps/agent-desk and apps/shared-inbox) that share the same module layout.
cases.why: The search term is split into at most six words and each one is pushed onto `params` as its own `%word%` pattern with a matching `$n` placeholder in the clause list, so no part of the client's term ever reaches the statement text. The only interpolated fragments are the joined placeholder clauses and an ORDER BY chosen from the constant ORDERS map.

cases.architecture: Socket.IO gateway plus a raw `ws` widget bridge and Express SSE routes for a support desk, over Postgres and Mongo: two sibling deployments (apps/agent-desk and apps/shared-inbox) that share the same module layout.
cases.why: The whole client-supplied `filter` object is spread into the Mongo query, so any key and any value the agent's console sends becomes part of the selector - `{"assigneeId":{"$ne":null}}` or a `$where` clause are both accepted. Worse, the spread comes *after* `orgId` and `deletedAt`, so a filter containing `orgId` overwrites the tenant scope and reads another organisation's ticket projections, including requester names.

cases.architecture: Socket.IO gateway plus a raw `ws` widget bridge and Express SSE routes for a support desk, over Postgres and Mongo: two sibling deployments (apps/agent-desk and apps/shared-inbox) that share the same module layout.
cases.why: The view is compiled rather than merged: only keys in the FACETS allow-list survive, and every value must be a string matching an anchored character class, so no operator object can ever reach `find()`. The tenant scope and the soft-delete predicate are written after the compiled facets, which means a facet named `orgId` cannot displace them.

cases.architecture: Socket.IO gateway plus a raw `ws` widget bridge and Express SSE routes for a support desk, over Postgres and Mongo: two sibling deployments (apps/agent-desk and apps/shared-inbox) that share the same module layout.
cases.why: The ticket is selected on its id alone: the query has no organisation predicate and no grant join, and nothing after it compares the row to `socket.data.session`. The UUID check only constrains the shape. Any authenticated agent - of any tenant - who has a ticket id therefore receives the subject, the requester's name and email address and the first page of the timeline, and the `socket.join` below also subscribes them to every later update on that ticket.

cases.architecture: Socket.IO gateway plus a raw `ws` widget bridge and Express SSE routes for a support desk, over Postgres and Mongo: two sibling deployments (apps/agent-desk and apps/shared-inbox) that share the same module layout.
cases.why: The authorisation is the join: the ticket row only materialises when `ticket_grants` holds a live, unrevoked grant for the socket's own agent id, which is bound as a parameter from `socket.data.session`. A ticket the caller has no grant on returns no rows and is answered with `ticket_not_found`, so the room is never joined and no panel is serialised.

cases.architecture: Socket.IO gateway plus a raw `ws` widget bridge and Express SSE routes for a support desk, over Postgres and Mongo: two sibling deployments (apps/agent-desk and apps/shared-inbox) that share the same module layout.
cases.why: The request's own `Origin` header is echoed back as `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` - falling back to `*` when absent - and paired with `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true`. That combination lets any site the agent visits open this EventSource with the desk session cookie attached and read the tenant's live queue counters cross-origin; the reflection makes the allow-list effectively universal, and there is no `Vary: Origin` either.

cases.architecture: Socket.IO gateway plus a raw `ws` widget bridge and Express SSE routes for a support desk, over Postgres and Mongo: two sibling deployments (apps/agent-desk and apps/shared-inbox) that share the same module layout.
cases.why: The credentialed grant is only issued when the request's Origin is an exact member of the two-entry STREAM_ORIGINS set; anything else - including a request with no Origin at all - gets no CORS headers, so no third-party page can read the stream. `Vary: Origin` is set as well, so a shared cache cannot hand one shell's grant to another.
